claim: The transactional outbox pattern addresses how to update the database and send a message atomically.
quote: How to atomically update the database and send messages to a message broker?
notes: Chris Richardson, microservices.io. Forces section adds: '2PC is not an option.'

claim: Outbox solution: write the message to the database in the same transaction as the business change; a separate process sends it to the broker.
quote: The solution is for the service that sends the message to first store the message in the database as part of the transaction that updates the business entities. A separate process then sends the messages to the message broker.

claim: The outbox message relay can publish a message more than once (crash after publishing, before recording), so consumers must be idempotent.
quote: Message relay might publish a message more than once. It might, for example, crash after publishing a message but before recording the fact that it has done so. When it restarts, it will then publish the message again. As a result, a message consumer must be idempotent, perhaps by tracking the IDs of the messages that it has already processed.
notes: Quoted from 'Message relay' onward within a bullet of the Resulting context section.

claim: Polling publisher: the relay polls the outbox table; drawback: ordering is tricky.
quote: Publish messages by polling the database’s outbox table.
notes: Benefits: 'Works with any SQL database'. Drawbacks listed: 'Tricky to publish events in order', 'Not all NoSQL databases support this pattern'.

claim: Transaction log tailing: read the database's transaction log (MySQL binlog, Postgres WAL, DynamoDB streams) and publish outbox inserts.
quote: Tail the database transaction log and publish each message/event inserted into the outbox to the message broker.
notes: Mechanisms listed: 'MySQL binlog', 'Postgres WAL', 'AWS DynamoDB table streams'. Drawbacks include 'Requires database specific solutions' and 'Tricky to avoid duplicate publishing'.

claim: Idempotent consumer: insert the message id into a PROCESSED_MESSAGE table inside the same transaction; a duplicate fails the primary key and is discarded.
quote: After starting the database transaction, the message handler inserts the message’s ID into the PROCESSED_MESSAGE table. Since the (subscriberId, messageID) is the PROCESSED_MESSAGE table’s primary key the INSERT will fail if the message has been already processed successfully.

claim: A saga is a sequence of local transactions; on failure, compensating transactions undo prior steps.
quote: A saga is a sequence of local transactions. Each local transaction updates the database and publishes a message or event to trigger the next local transaction in the saga. If a local transaction fails because it violates a business rule then the saga executes a series of compensating transactions that undo the changes that were made by the preceding local transactions.

claim: Two ways to coordinate sagas: choreography (events) and orchestration (an orchestrator tells participants what to do).
quote: Choreography - each local transaction publishes domain events that trigger local transactions in other services Orchestration - an orchestrator (object) tells the participants what local transactions to execute
notes: Original is a two-item bulleted list; hyphens are the page's own.

claim: Saga drawbacks: no automatic rollback, and no isolation between concurrent sagas.
quote: Lack of isolation (the “I” in ACID) - the lack of isolation means that there’s risk that the concurrent execution of multiple sagas and transactions can use data anomalies.
notes: 'can use data anomalies' is the page's own typo (sic). Other drawback: 'Lack of automatic rollback - a developer must design compensating transactions that explicitly undo changes made earlier in a saga rather than relying on the automatic rollback feature of ACID transactions'.

claim: Debezium's Outbox Event Router expects an outbox table with columns id, aggregatetype, aggregateid, type, payload.
quote: To apply the default outbox event router SMT configuration, your outbox table is assumed to have the following columns: Column | Type | Modifiers --------------+------------------------+----------- id | uuid | not null aggregatetype | character varying(255) | not null aggregateid | character varying(255) | not null type | character varying(255) | not null payload | jsonb |
notes: Table rendered as text. aggregatetype is appended to the topic name (default outbox.event.${routedByValue}); aggregateid becomes the message key by default.

claim: The outbox event id travels as a message header and can be used by consumers to remove duplicates.
quote: Contains the unique ID of the event. In an outbox message, this value is a header. You can use this ID, for example, to remove duplicate messages.

claim: Debezium's Postgres connector reads changes through Postgres logical decoding of the write-ahead log; pgoutput is the standard built-in output plug-in.
quote: Logical decoding extracts data changes from the PostgreSQL write-ahead log (WAL) and converts them to a format that Debezium can consume.
notes: Also: 'pgoutput The standard logical decoding output plug-in in PostgreSQL 10+. It is maintained by the PostgreSQL community, and used by PostgreSQL itself for logical replication.' Server setting: 'wal_level=logical'.

claim: Debezium never loses events but after a fault may emit duplicates: at-least-once delivery in abnormal situations.
quote: When the system is operating normally or being managed carefully then Debezium provides exactly once delivery of every change event record. If a fault does happen then the system does not lose any events. However, while it is recovering from the fault, it’s possible that the connector might emit some duplicate change events. In these abnormal situations, Debezium, like Kafka, provides at least once delivery of change events.
notes: Section 'Behavior when things go wrong'. Crash case: 'the new replacement tasks might generate some of the same change events that were processed just prior to the crash. The number of duplicate events depends on the offset flush period and the volume of data changes just before the crash.' Debezium docs also list an opt-in 'Exactly-once delivery' feature (not checked here).

claim: Dual write problem: writing to the database and to Kafka separately can leave one done and the other not, because no shared transaction spans both.
quote: Simply issuing these two requests may lead to potential inconsistencies, though. The reason being that we cannot have one shared transaction that would span the service’s database as well as Apache Kafka, as the latter doesn’t support to be enlisted in distributed (XA) transactions. So in unfortunate circumstances it might happen that we end up with having the new purchase order persisted in the local database, but not having sent the corresponding message to Kafka (e.g. due to some networking issue). Or, the other way around, we might have sent the message to Kafka but failed to persist the purchase order in the local database.
notes: Gunnar Morling, Debezium blog, section 'The Issue of Dual Writes'.

claim: The outbox avoids the dual write by modifying only the service's own database.
quote: By only modifying a single resource - the source service’s own database - it avoids any potential inconsistencies of altering multiple resources at the same time which don’t share one common transactional context (the database and Apache Kafka).

claim: PostgreSQL logical decoding turns the write-ahead log into an application-level change stream (the basis of change data capture).
quote: Logical decoding is the process of extracting all persistent changes to a database's tables into a coherent, easy to understand format which can be interpreted without detailed knowledge of the database's internal state. In PostgreSQL, logical decoding is implemented by decoding the contents of the write-ahead log, which describe changes on a storage level, into an application-specific form such as a stream of tuples or SQL statements.

claim: PostgreSQL's two-phase commit primitive is not meant for applications; a prepared transaction left hanging keeps its locks.
quote: PREPARE TRANSACTION is not intended for use in applications or interactive sessions. Its purpose is to allow an external transaction manager to perform atomic global transactions across multiple databases or other transactional resources. Unless you're writing a transaction manager, you probably shouldn't be using PREPARE TRANSACTION.
notes: Caution box on same page: 'It is unwise to leave transactions in the prepared state for a long time.' and 'Keep in mind also that the transaction continues to hold whatever locks it held.'

claim: Garcia-Molina and Salem (1987) define a saga: a long-lived transaction written as a sequence of transactions that can interleave with others; either all complete or compensating transactions amend a partial execution.
quote: To alleviate these problems we propose the notion of a saga. A LLT is a saga if it can be written as a sequence of transactions that can be interleaved with other transactions. The database management system guarantees that either all the transactions in a saga are successfully completed or compensating transactions are run to amend a partial execution.
notes: Abstract. The PDF is a scan; its text layer has OCR errors ('1s', 'm', 'compensatmg') and no periods; quote is the OCR text with obvious OCR errors corrected and sentence periods restored. LLT = long lived transaction. Paper also notes: 'other transactions might see the effects of a partial saga execution' (no isolation).

claim: In the original sagas paper, other transactions may see a partially executed saga; compensation does not notify them.
quote: other transactions might see the effects of a partial saga execution. When a compensating transaction Ci is run, no effort is made to notify or abort transactions that might have seen the results of Ti before they were compensated for by Ci.
notes: OCR-corrected from scan (original OCR: 'When a compensatmg transaction C, 1s run, no effort 1s made to notify or abort transactions that nught have seen the results of T, before they were compensated for by c, 1'). Subscripts rendered as Ci/Ti.

claim: Classic two-phase commit blocks if the coordinator fails; Paxos Commit avoids that with 2F+1 coordinators.
quote: The distributed transaction commit problem requires reaching agreement on whether a transaction is committed or aborted. The classic Two-Phase Commit protocol blocks if the coordinator fails. Fault-tolerant consensus algorithms also reach agreement, but do not block whenever any majority of the processes are working.
published: 2004-08-14 (arXiv); Jim Gray and Leslie Lamport, 'Consensus on Transaction Commit', MSR-TR-2003-96; later ACM TODS 2006

claim: Event sourcing: capture every change to application state as an event object, stored in order, for the lifetime of the application state.
quote: The fundamental idea of Event Sourcing is that of ensuring every change to the state of an application is captured in an event object, and that these event objects are themselves stored in the sequence they were applied for the same lifetime as the application state itself.
notes: Summary line at top: 'Capture all changes to an application state as a sequence of events.'

claim: CQRS uses a different model to update information than to read it.
quote: CQRS stands for Command Query Responsibility Segregation. It's a pattern that I first heard described by Greg Young. At its heart is the notion that you can use a different model to update information than the model you use to read information.

claim: Fowler warns that for most systems CQRS adds risky complexity.
quote: For some situations, this separation can be valuable, but beware that for most systems CQRS adds risky complexity.
notes: Also on the page: 'Despite these benefits, you should be very cautious about using CQRS. Many information systems fit well with the notion of an information base that is updated in the same way that it's read, adding CQRS to such a system can add significant complexity.' and 'the majority of cases I've run into have not been so good, with CQRS seen as a significant force for getting a software system into serious difficulties.' Key phrases verified against page HTML.

claim: Microsoft's guidance: event sourcing is complex and costly to migrate to or from; for most systems traditional data management is enough.
quote: Event sourcing is a complex pattern that introduces significant trade-offs. It changes how you store data, handle concurrency, evolve schemas, and query state. It's costly to migrate to or from an event sourcing solution, and after you adopt the pattern, it constrains future design decisions in the parts of the system that use it. Adopt event sourcing when its benefits, like auditability and historical reconstruction, justify the pattern's complexity. For most systems and most parts of a system, traditional data management is sufficient.

claim: When event sourcing is not suitable: plain CRUD, prototypes/MVPs, systems needing real-time consistent views, static reference data, teams new to event-driven design.
quote: Systems have straightforward CRUD operations that don't require auditability, replay, or historical reconstruction of state. The operational overhead of an event store isn't justified if the only requirement is current-state reads and writes.
notes: First bullet under 'This pattern might not be suitable when:'. Others: 'Prototypes, minimum viable products (MVPs), or systems have short expected lifespans.'; 'Systems require consistency and real-time updates to the views of the data. Eventual consistency between the event store and projections is inherent to event sourcing.'; 'Domains in which data is mostly static or for reference, such as lookup tables or catalogs.'; 'Teams don't have experience in event-driven architectures.'

claim: Kafka is not an event store: it lacks per-entity stream queries and optimistic concurrency.
quote: Don't confuse an event store with an eventstream message broker. Message brokers such as Apache Kafka typically lack per-entity stream queries and optimistic concurrency. They work well as a distribution layer to fan out events to projections and external consumers, but they aren't a substitute for an event store.
notes: Useful correction to the common belief that 'Kafka is an event store'.

claim: Event delivery to consumers is typically at least once, so handlers must be idempotent.
quote: Event delivery to consumers is typically at least once, so consumers can receive the same event more than once. Event handlers must be idempotent so processing a duplicate event doesn't change the outcome.

claim: Two Generals (Gray's 'generals paradox'): with messengers that can get lost, no fixed-length protocol lets both generals be sure to march together.
quote: There is a simple proof that: no fixed length protocol exists: Let P be the shortest such protocol. Suppose the last messenger in P gets lost. Then either this messenger is useless or one of the generals doesn't get a needed message. By the minimality of P, the last message is not useless so one of the general doesn't march if the last message is lost. This contradiction proves that no such protocol P exists.
published: 1977/1978 (Jim Gray, 'Notes on Data Base Operating Systems', IBM Research Report RJ2188, in Operating Systems: An Advanced Course, LNCS 60, 1978)
notes: Section 5.8.3.3.1 'THE GENERALS PARADOX'. Setup: 'The generals are encamped only a short distance apart, but due to technical difficulties, they can communicate only via runners. These messengers have a flaw, every time they venture out of camp they stand some chance of getting lost'. Gray then relates it to commit processing (cash terminal plus account debit). The earlier origin is Akkoyunlu, Ekanadham and Huber, SOSP 1975 (not fetched; ACM DL returned 403).

claim: Inbox pattern: the receiver records incoming message ids (keyed by MessageId) so a redelivered message is not processed twice; often combined with an outbox.
quote: The Consumer Outbox is a combination of an inbox and an outbox. The inbox is used to keep track of received messages to guarantee exactly-once consumer behavior.
notes: MassTransit documentation. Also: 'As a message is received, the inbox is used to lock the message by MessageId.' Caveat: 'exactly-once consumer behavior' here means effects applied once via deduplication over at-least-once delivery, not exactly-once delivery on the wire. The two quoted sentences are adjacent on the page as extracted from HTML; verify adjacency if quoting as one block.

claim: NServiceBus's outbox deduplicates incoming messages by MessageId, the same idea as an inbox.
quote: NServiceBus uses the message identity( MessageId ) to deduplicate messages.
notes: Spacing '( MessageId )' is an artifact of HTML-to-text extraction; on the page MessageId is code-formatted. Also: 'If the system is processing a high volume of messages, having a long deduplication time frame will increase the storage space required by the outbox.'

claim: Stripe retries webhook deliveries for up to three days with exponential backoff in live mode (three times over a few hours in a sandbox).
quote: Stripe attempts to deliver events to your destination for up to three days with an exponential back off in live mode.
notes: Also: 'We retry event deliveries created in a sandbox three times over the course of a few hours.'

claim: Stripe may deliver the same event more than once; dedupe by logging processed event ids.
quote: Webhook endpoints might occasionally receive the same event more than once. You can guard against duplicated event receipts by logging the event IDs you’ve processed, and then not processing already-logged events.
notes: Next sentences: 'In some cases, two separate Event objects are generated and sent. To identify these duplicates, use the ID of the object in data.object along with the event.type.' So event-id dedupe alone is not always enough.

claim: Stripe does not guarantee webhook events arrive in the order they were generated.
quote: Stripe doesn’t guarantee the delivery of events in the order that they’re generated.
notes: Also: 'Make sure that your event destination isn’t dependent on receiving events in a specific order.' and 'Don’t use created to determine event order or whether you’ve already processed an event.'

claim: Webhook receivers should acknowledge quickly and do slow work afterwards.
quote: Your endpoint must quickly return a successful status code ( 2xx ) before any complex logic that could cause a timeout.
notes: Spacing around 2xx is an extraction artifact (code-formatted on the page).

claim: GitHub does not automatically retry failed webhook deliveries; you redeliver manually or via the REST API.
quote: GitHub does not automatically redeliver failed deliveries.
notes: Correction to a common belief that all webhook providers retry. 'You can manually redeliver failed deliveries.' and 'Use the GitHub REST API to redeliver any deliveries that failed.'

claim: GitHub expects a 2XX within 10 seconds or treats the delivery as failed; it suggests queueing the payload for async processing.
quote: Your server should respond with a 2XX response within 10 seconds of receiving a webhook delivery. If your server takes longer than that to respond, then GitHub terminates the connection and considers the delivery a failure. In order to respond in a timely manner, you may want to set up a queue to process webhook payloads asynchronously.

claim: The X-GitHub-Delivery header is unique per event and stays the same on redelivery, so it works as an idempotency key.
quote: To protect against replay attacks, you can use the X-GitHub-Delivery header to ensure that each delivery is unique per event.
notes: Note on page: 'If you request a redelivery, the X-GitHub-Delivery header will be the same as in the original delivery.'

claim: Svix retries failed webhooks on a fixed schedule from immediately up to 10 hours apart (about 27 to 28 hours of attempts in total).
quote: Each message is attempted based on the following schedule, where each period is started following the failure of the preceding attempt: Immediately 5 seconds 5 minutes 30 minutes 2 hours 5 hours 10 hours 10 hours (in addition to the previous)
notes: List flattened from HTML. Sum of waits is about 27.6 hours (my arithmetic, not stated on page).

claim: OpenAI Responses API background mode runs long tasks asynchronously (background=true) so clients poll instead of holding a connection open.
quote: Background mode enables you to execute long-running tasks on models like GPT-5.2 and GPT-5.2 Pro reliably, without having to worry about timeouts or other connectivity issues. Background mode kicks off these tasks asynchronously, and developers can poll response objects to check status over time.
notes: Model names on the page change over time.

claim: Poll while status is queued or in_progress; any other status is terminal.
quote: Keep polling while the request is in the queued or in_progress state. When it leaves these states, it has reached a final (terminal) state.
notes: Terminal states (completed, failed, cancelled, incomplete) are not listed in this sentence. Cancel endpoint: POST /v1/responses/{id}/cancel.

claim: A background response can also be streamed; track each event's sequence_number as a cursor and resume after a dropped connection with starting_after.
quote: You can create a background Response and start streaming events from it right away. This may be helpful if you expect the client to drop the stream and want the option of picking it back up later. To do this, create a Response with both background and stream set to true . You will want to keep track of a “cursor” corresponding to the sequence_number you receive in each streaming event.
notes: Resume example on page: GET https://api.openai.com/v1/responses/resp_123?stream=true&starting_after=42. Also: 'Currently, the time to first token you receive from a background response is higher than what you receive from a synchronous one.' And: 'You can only start a new stream from a background response if you created it with stream=true.'

claim: Background responses are stored temporarily (roughly 10 minutes) to allow polling; kept longer only with store=true; this matters for Zero Data Retention.
quote: Response data is temporarily stored to disk for roughly 10 minutes to enable asynchronous execution and polling.
notes: Also: 'Background responses are retained after the polling period only when store=true is explicitly provided. If store is omitted or set to false for a background request, the response is deleted after roughly 10 minutes.' and 'Background requests from Zero Data Retention (ZDR) projects run with store=false.'

claim: OpenAI Batch API: asynchronous groups of requests at 50% lower cost with a 24-hour completion window.
quote: Learn how to use OpenAI’s Batch API to send asynchronous groups of requests with 50% lower costs, a separate pool of significantly higher rate limits, and a clear 24-hour turnaround time.
notes: Also: 'For now, the completion window can only be set to 24h.' Unfinished requests get error code 'batch_expired'.

claim: Anthropic Message Batches: 50% price, most batches finish in under an hour, expire after 24 hours, limit 100,000 requests or 256 MB.
quote: This approach is well-suited to tasks that do not require immediate responses, with most batches finishing in less than 1 hour while reducing costs by 50% and increasing throughput.
notes: Also: 'Batches expire if processing does not complete within 24 hours.'; 'A Message Batch is limited to either 100,000 Message requests or 256 MB in size, whichever is reached first.'; 'Batch results are available for 29 days after creation.'

claim: Anthropic batch size limit.
quote: A Message Batch is limited to either 100,000 Message requests or 256 MB in size, whichever is reached first.

claim: Claude's Messages API streams responses with server-sent events when stream is true.
quote: When creating a Message, you can set "stream": true to incrementally stream the response using server-sent events (SSE).

claim: Temporal's integration with the OpenAI Agents SDK makes agent runs durable: it records progress and activity results so a crashed run resumes where it left off, with retries.
quote: Remember what I said earlier about Temporal picking up where it left off in the event of a crash? This is how you get that Durable Execution: Temporal keeps track of application progress and stores all Activity results, and that’s how it can simply keep going when latent troubles have been resolved.
published: 2025 (Public Preview announcement; exact date not found in page text)
notes: Also: 'Your app crashes when it’s just about done with a long-running task? Restart it, and Temporal will see to it that it picks up where it left off, saving you compute and token costs!' Vendor blog (Temporal), so promotional framing.

claim: Vercel AI SDK resumable streams: closing a tab or refreshing only drops the HTTP connection, not the generation; resuming needs persisted messages and active streams (e.g. Redis).
quote: In a resumable stream setup, client-side aborts are treated as disconnects. Closing a tab, refreshing the page, or calling stop() only closes the current HTTP connection and should not cancel the underlying generation.
notes: Also: 'Stream resumption requires persistence for messages and active streams in your application. The AI SDK provides tools to connect to storage, but you need to set up the storage yourself.' You build 'Redis to store the UIMessage stream'.

claim: Cloudflare Workflows: durable multi-step execution with automatic retries and state persisted for minutes to weeks.
quote: With Workflows, you can build applications that chain together multiple steps, automatically retry failed tasks, and persist state for minutes, hours, or even weeks - with no infrastructure to manage.
notes: Agents SDK page (https://developers.cloudflare.com/agents/) describes its runtime as 'Durable identity, state, connections, scheduling, and recovery.'
